```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_ne <- requireNamespace("rnaturalearth", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("rnaturalearthdata", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("sf", quietly = TRUE)
has_hires <- has_ne && requireNamespace("rnaturalearthhires", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = has_ne)
```

```{r setup, eval = TRUE}
library(geoscales)
```

## The package ships no maps

`geoscales` contains integration code, not data. There is no `data/`
directory and no bundled boundaries. A provider fetches a source table; the
package records what was fetched.

```{r, eval = TRUE}
list_geoscale_providers()
```

Natural Earth is the default provider because its country table is *already*
a wide leaftable — one `sf` object carries the whole nest as columns:

```
continent (8) -> region_un -> subregion (22) -> sovereignt
              -> admin / adm0_a3 (177) -> geounit -> subunit
```

with `pop_est` and `gdp_md` as ready-made weights.

```{r}
gs <- ne_geoscale(scale = 110)
gs
```

## Aggregating up

Iceland serves as the running example. It sits in Northern Europe:

```{r}
lf <- S7::prop(gs, "leaftable")
lf[lf$country == "ISL", c("continent", "subregion", "country", "pop_est")]
```

Rolling population up from countries to sub-regions is one call. `rule = "sum"`
because population is *extensive* — it adds up:

```{r}
pop <- data.frame(country = lf$country, pop = lf$pop_est)
pop <- pop[!is.na(pop$country), ]

agg <- recast_geoscale(pop, gs, source = "country", target = "subregion", rule = "sum")
agg[agg$subregion == "Northern Europe", ]
```

## Disaggregating down

The same verb runs the other way. Going down, `rule = "sum"` splits a total in
proportion to a weight, so the total is conserved:

```{r}
ne <- agg[agg$subregion == "Northern Europe", ]

back <- recast_geoscale(ne, gs, source = "subregion", target = "country",
                   rule = "sum", weight = "pop_est")
head(back[order(-back$pop), ], 4)
```

Because the split uses the same quantity that was aggregated, the round trip
is exact:

```{r}
back$pop[back$country == "ISL"]
sum(back$pop) == sum(ne$pop)
```

**Aggregation and disaggregation are one operation.** Direction follows the geoframe ranks, and `recast_geoscale()` routes through the leaf
layer either way.

## Iceland's own regions

Natural Earth's admin-1 layer gives sub-country areas. This needs
`rnaturalearthhires`, which is **not on CRAN**:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("rnaturalearthhires",
                 repos = "https://ropensci.r-universe.dev")
```

```{r, eval = has_hires}
s <- ne_source(geoframe = "states", country = "Iceland")
d <- as.data.frame(s)
nrow(d)
```

Nine admin-1 areas — but Iceland has eight regions. `Reykjavik` and the surrounding
capital area are separate admin-1 features that belong to the same region,
which Natural Earth records in `gn_name`. That gives a genuinely **ragged**
hierarchy: one group with two children, seven with one.

```{r, eval = has_hires}
isl <- data.frame(
  country    = "ISL",
  landshluti = d$gn_name,       # Iceland's eight regions
  admin1     = d$iso_3166_2,    # the nine admin-1 areas
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

g <- geoscale_from_leaftable(
  isl, geoframes = c("country", "landshluti", "admin1"),
  leaf = "admin1", name = "iceland"
)
g <- attach_geometry_geoscale(g, s, by = "iso_3166_2", geoframe = "admin1")
g <- add_area_geoscale(g, name = "km2")
g
```

The Capital Region is the one that has two areas under it:

```{r, eval = has_hires}
geoscale_children(g, "landshluti", "Hofudborgarsvadi")
geoscale_nests(g, "landshluti", "admin1")
```

### Up: areas to regions to country

```{r, eval = has_hires}
set.seed(1)
x <- data.frame(admin1 = geoscale_regions(g, "admin1"),
                generation = round(runif(9, 50, 500)))

recast_geoscale(x, g, source = "admin1", target = "landshluti", rule = "sum")
```

```{r, eval = has_hires}
recast_geoscale(x, g, source = "admin1", target = "country", rule = "sum")
sum(x$generation)
```

### Down: a national total split by area

```{r, eval = has_hires}
tot <- data.frame(country = "ISL", demand = 1000)

dd <- recast_geoscale(tot, g, source = "country", target = "admin1",
                 rule = "sum", weight = "km2")
dd[order(-dd$demand), ]
```

The Capital Region areas receive almost nothing, because they are small in
area, although they hold most of Iceland's population and would consume most
of its electricity. **Area is rarely the right weight for demand.**
`recast_geoscale()` therefore requires an explicit `weight =`; with a
population column on the leaftable, that column would be the weight.

An *intensive* quantity must not be summed at all; `weighted_mean` copies
going down and weight-averages going up:

```{r, eval = has_hires}
cf <- data.frame(admin1 = geoscale_regions(g, "admin1"),
                 cf = round(runif(9, 0.2, 0.5), 3))

recast_geoscale(cf, g, "admin1", "landshluti", rule = "weighted_mean", weight = "km2")
```

### Geometry follows the geoframes

`geoscale_geometry()` dissolves the leaves up to the requested geoframe, so the
nine areas become eight regions:

```{r, eval = has_hires}
shp <- geoscale_geometry(g, geoframe = "landshluti")
nrow(shp)
```

```{r, eval = has_hires && requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE), fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
gg_geoscale(g, type = "map", geoframe = "landshluti")
```

## Other providers

The same interface accepts any source. Register one with
`register_geoscale_provider()`, or pass an `sf` object straight to
`geoscale_from_provider()`. Natural candidates are `giscoR` (authoritative
NUTS for Europe), `geodata`/GADM (admin-2 and admin-3 — note its licence
forbids commercial use) and `tigris` (US Census).
